correctness.rationale: Independently identify the degree-three part with V* via x wedge c = c(x) omega. For odd parts (u,c) and (v,d) the normalized commutator is (u wedge v, d(u)-c(v)); the two independent even parts multiply every odd-pair count by q^16. If u is nonzero, the fixed-first-input image is (u wedge V) direct sum k omega of dimension four, so there are q^4 odd second inputs over each reachable target. If u=0 and c is nonzero the image is just k omega (q^7 preimages); if both vanish there are q^8 preimages of zero only. For a fixed nonzero simple bivector the possible nonzero u are precisely the q^2-1 nonzero vectors of its plane, with q^4 freely chosen c, giving odd-pair size q^8(q^2-1). A nonsimple bivector is unreachable. For a=0 the nonzero-u contribution is (q^4-1)q^8 and the u=0, c nonzero contribution is (q^4-1)q^7, for every b; at b=0 one adds q^8. These yield the stated D and the ordinary-commutator counts by invertible rescaling. Nonzero simple bivectors number (q-1) times the Gaussian coefficient [4 choose 2]_q and every b occurs, giving the stated image size. Fixed-first-input ranks 0,1,4 for the three cases give centralizer sizes q^16,q^15,q^12 and respective counts q^8,q^8(q^4-1),q^12(q^4-1). The zero fiber divided by q^32 equals the stated probability. The degree-two and top-degree basis wedges span the indicated commutator subspace; alternating normal form writes every bivector as at most two simple terms, and e_12+e_34 is not simple in odd characteristic. In dimensions at most three all bivectors are simple or zero and there is no top term, so every element of the span is a single commutator (also zero in the trivial-span cases). No primality assumption is used. The frozen prime-field script was inspected, not executed; its finite checks are not needed for the proof over all odd prime powers.
